what_its_for: Gemcitabine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including pancreatic cancer, lung cancer (non-small cell), breast cancer, and ovarian cancer. It works by slowing down or stopping the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_to_take: Gemcitabine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT take this medicine at home as a pill or injection. Each infusion usually takes about 30 minutes, but your doctor may adjust the time. You will likely receive treatments on a schedule, such as once a week for several weeks, followed by a rest week. Always attend all of your scheduled appointments.
dosing: Your dose is calculated based on your body size (height and weight) and the type of cancer being treated. Your doctor or care team will determine the exact dose that is right for you. Common schedules include receiving the infusion once a week for 3 weeks, followed by 1 week off, then repeating the cycle. Do not try to adjust your dose on your own. Your doctor may lower your dose or delay treatment if you experience certain side effects, such as low blood cell counts.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, contact your cancer care team as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your team will help you reschedule and adjust your treatment plan safely. Missing doses can affect how well the treatment works, so it is very important to keep all appointments.
storage: Gemcitabine is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you are given any supplies or materials related to your treatment, follow the specific storage instructions provided by your care team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as gemcitabine can lower your immune system and make it easier to get sick. Avoid crowded places when possible. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the live flu nasal spray or shingles vaccine) during treatment without asking your doctor first. Avoid drinking alcohol excessively, as it may worsen side effects. Tell your doctor before taking any new medicines, including vitamins, supplements, or over-the-counter drugs. Women who are pregnant or could become pregnant should avoid this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after finishing. Men should use birth control for at least 3 months after treatment. Do not breastfeed while taking gemcitabine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this could be a sign of serious infection); chills, sweating, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; shortness of breath or difficulty breathing; chest pain; severe swelling in your hands, feet, or legs; signs of a serious lung problem such as new or worsening cough or feeling short of breath; signs of kidney problems such as little or no urination; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or mouth sores that are very painful or prevent eating. Also call your doctor if you feel unusually tired, notice a rash or skin changes, or have any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Gemcitabine starts working right away at the cellular level, but it may take several weeks or cycles of treatment before you or your doctor notice results, such as a shrinking tumor or improved symptoms. Your doctor will check how well the treatment is working through regular blood tests and imaging scans (such as CT scans). Be patient and continue all scheduled treatments, even if you do not feel immediate changes. Everyone responds differently to chemotherapy.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to the side effects of gemcitabine, especially low blood counts. Your doctor will monitor you closely and may adjust your dose. Kidney or liver problems: Gemcitabine is processed by the liver and kidneys. If you have kidney or liver disease, tell your doctor before starting treatment, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Pregnancy: Gemcitabine can seriously harm an unborn baby and should NOT be used during pregnancy. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant during treatment. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while receiving gemcitabine, as the medicine may pass into breast milk and harm the baby. Children: Gemcitabine is not commonly used in children, and safety in pediatric patients has not been fully established. Use in children should only occur under the supervision of a specialist.
